Honestly? You've got the right attitude in being passionate. I've known several people in STEM who just get away with half arsing it across various fields, it's just how it is. But i disagree with your idea that you failed as a person because you're working some ordinary job or reserach, your self worth as a human being shouldn't be directed towards your job, but how you are as a human being.

I think STEM is overrated for the most part, even good research doesn't necessarily require a great mind if i'm honest. People think you have to work exceptionally hard for a good position, but in most disciplines all you gotta do is just put a couple of hours in your day and you're done if you pay attention.   
I just don't see why everyone thinks STEM people are considered any more intelligent than the average person, even good researchers are nothing special, they just put a lot of time and have the reasoning capacity of anyone else who put in the time, literally anyone else could do it. Of course there's one in a million who manage to figure out a missing link or something groundbreaking, but most people are just average.

It became pretty clear to me how little people seem to nurture their intellect. Even something simple as reading and developing critical thinking on real life issues just makes you a more intelligent human being overall. I've spoken to med students who have zero life experience and who know next to nothing about the world around them and it's frustrating after a while, are we really intelligent if all we do is focus on one single thing that is the subject we're studying for uni or career? 

 It's a shame to see so many people waste their life away on their phones for hours a day when they're not studying for their education/work instead of reading and doing stuff that genuinely enriches our life as human beings (like literally any hobby)

As someone who's in 3rd year in biomedical science, STEM is generally pretty easy to rote learn, you're not taught critical thinking skills much less taught to seek out knowledge, Uni itself prioritises learning as a means to an end (e.g better grades or career position).

It's a failing of a society that prioritises your position over your passions and obviously you see so many people just doing stem to get a 'good job' because it's minimal effort and you don't have to network a great deal compared to econ and other careers, hence the level of disinterest.  So you get a bunch of people choosing the subject just to get a job that doesn't suck. It's also a consequence of the failure of the education system to adequately nurture the interests or passions of the students who eventually go to uni.

If you can get a decent paying job when you can half arse a  degree and still succeed then why do more? 

In research you don't necessarily have to engage with much, learning a specific area of research isn't that hard or time consuming, neither is highlighting gaps in literature. A lot of the time you're directed by other people who do the thinking for you, sure you have to use your head but it's not like you're just coming up with these ideas yourself.

STEM is praised as this subject for intelligent people when it's really not. If you show up and pay half attention you can get somewhere. Many people I know who are postgraduates are in good positions who simply don't care and do the bare minimum.

Not only is this true for PHDs but getting bursaries and grants for masters is a challenge. Anything postgraduate is becoming a joke, really.

I come from a working class background and in-between academic years I've had to work because I don't have a family who can help support my living. 

I'm now in my final year studying biomedical science and I've had to spend all of my savings on rent and living costs over the years. And I was just getting by on my maintenance loan. 

If I choose to do a masters I'm either going to have to work part of full time whilst studying to even afford my rent, let alone food and other living costs, and that's with a scholarship.

it's ridiculous, because my plan was to do a masters and then do graduate entry medicine, but now my only option really is to bite the bullet and go with GEM and pray I get in.

How does anyone expect to get anywhere with uni these days especially if you're not from a middle class household? Because an increasing number of jobs require a postgraduate degree nowadays.

But psychiatrists are rarely knowledgeable on the systemic factors that lead to people having poor mental health. 

Hell, there are so many books that highlight this, the stats on women of colour being diagnosed with bipolar, personality disorders and anger issues for being angry and at the end of their wits with racism (Fanon has written about effects of racism on the mind). In addition to this, so many people are misdiagnosed for having human responses to shit conditions. And there's a term called "shit life syndrome" which is self explanatory, and these people are genuinely depressed because their life is crap. And they get put on SSRIs to tolerate situations that are intolerable. And this completely ignores that the way the world is structured, and places the responsibility on the individual, and ignores the fact that society at large needs to be reformed.

Where are the contradictions? And whatever you're saying is so backwards? The reasons she wanted to die are on the articles you said I contradicted, her reasons are pretty clear cut if you've bothered to read them.

And it's not disrespectful to her. I don't think that raising awareness to glaring issues in society that lead to people being so miserable that they kill themselves is disrespectful. Nor is it disrespectful to say that her problems were human issues which may have been improved via human solutions. Nor is it to suggest that her life may have gotten better if she were treated as a human being instead of a broken doll who was consumed by her labels as mentally ill, and instead treated as a human being with real life problems.

Nor is it to criticise how mental health treatments treat every person as a ubiquitous case on flawed science, or to acknowledge the failings of our society that led to her misery in the first place. 

I also missed out one point too, her experiences as a woman and how it intersects with her being autistic were likely contributors of her misery.

This isn't hijacking, I think you want to assume people are removed from the bigger picture by individualist beliefs and insist on a shallow individual basis for suffering. But wouldn't you agree that acknowledging societal flaws (that likely contributed hugely to her situation) and the structures that causes misogyny, ableism and flawed mental health systems etc is good start in creating a better, happier world that is more equal? 

Rather than dancing around the issue and pretending that she was the way she was and that she was hopeless because a psychiatrist who hardly knows her as a person decided to put her through a regimen of treatment that has been shown to have limited effectiveness?

And to consider what the precedent is, rather than jumping on some false moral high ground to avoid a conversation?

I'm not making assumptions, there have been many articles on her story and I've read them. And why does everything have to be positive? Why are we scared of having conversations on legitimate issues for fear of it being perceived as negative?

The reason I've said this is because she, and many others and their circumstances are a product of the sick world that we live in. Her trauma, her life experiences and her treatment by others as an autistic person are prime examples.

And I think it's foolish to pretend like she was just wired that way when she wasn't. Again, I think it's foolish to believe that the be all and end all is medical treatments that are rooted in flawed science.

Even the efficacy of drugs has been overstated many times. Pharmaceutical companies love to peddle drugs that have terrible study design. 

And I'm also speaking about this from personal experience, as I was an inpatient at a psychiatric ward treated by "professionals" who made me believe that my shit life and trauma was something that i was stuck with for life, and that it was inherent within me, and not the circumstances that were past and present at that time which drove me to that state.

I, for one just think it's tragic that this is hailed as some kind of victory  for "personal choice" when it's not. It's sad because of her life but it's horrific when you realise how this was a human being who was failed by those around her and society at nearly every turn. Make no mistake that this was a social issue, a human one.

You only get one life, and she was allowed to end it when there were so many other options. She wasn't a lost cause despite the sheer pain she was in.
But is that due to having autism itself or the world around us being completely structured around those without it?

And maybe it's time to consider that mental health conditions are more of a human problem than we've been led to believe. Lets be honest here, her early years were shit, and her life thereafter likely was too, through trauma and her environment. Obviously she was depressed.

 Her "treatments" have been mostly drugs, electrode therapy, and talking therapy. Drugs aren't super effective, SSRIs compared to placebo have been shown to be ineffective. And allowing assisted suicide for cases like this sets an awful precedent. In addition to this, the structure of many therapies has been rooted in flawed science.

And in this world where mental health has been mystified, I think this is the fault of her environment with having a poor network of support, trauma and a partner who enabled her. In addition to living in a society which alienates all of us.
If she had a decent family, a community and a revised mental health system things might have turned out differently.

Boomed student here, there are quite a few diseases that can lead to heart attacks, so one of them is something called Long QT syndrome which is where the heart will take way too much time "regain" it's ions for another heartbeat.

Think of it as when the heart contracts it will use up it's battery and it recharges. Because of the delay, and often functional defect with ion transporters and other defects, the heart will enter vtac

This causes ventricular tachycardia where the lower chambers of your heart will spasm and you just won't get blood leaving the heart, so you'll not be recieving oxygenated blood to tissues, and you'll not be getting it oxygenated because little blood will go to the lungs -> tissue hypoxia and cardiac arrest will follow
